checks.claim: Key: the seed-grown meadow holds more biodiversity, for the variety in its genes (genetic diversity is one of biodiversity's levels)
checks.note: Grokipedia: biodiversity is counted at 'three hierarchical levels: genetic diversity, species diversity, and ecosystem diversity'; genetic diversity is 'the variation in genetic makeup within a population or species'.

checks.claim: A plant grown from a cutting is a clone with its parent's genes; seed-grown plants carry recombined, varied genes
checks.note: 'the new plant is a genetic clone of the parent'; cuttings 'produce genetically identical clones without such recombination'.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: neither, for both hold the same 20 species (species count alone)
checks.note: Wrong: species richness is only one of the three levels; the meadows differ at the genetic level.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: neither, for both hold as many plants
checks.note: Wrong: number of individuals is not biodiversity; within-species genetic variety differs.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: neither, for each species' plants look alike
checks.note: Wrong: genetic variety need not show in appearance; the seed-grown plants differ in their genes.

checks.claim: Context: biodiversity counted at three levels (genes, species, ecosystems); often taken to mean species number alone
checks.note: Three levels confirmed. The common reduction to species number is a documented student misconception (writer's MDPI 2019 source); stated in the context only as a common belief.

checks.claim: David Tilman and John A. Downing, over 200 grassland plots at Cedar Creek, Minnesota, measured for years before the drought
checks.note: Tilman D. and Downing J.A., 'Biodiversity and stability in grasslands', Nature 367:363-365 (1994); 207 plots (Tilman 1996 abstract); the e001 plots began in 1982 (Wikipedia, G. David Tilman: 'more than 200 grassland plots').

checks.claim: The worst drought in 50 years struck in 1987 and 1988
checks.note: The paper: 'the most severe drought of the past 50 years occurred (1987-1988)' (also in search snippets of the Nature abstract).

checks.claim: Plots with more species lost a smaller share of their growth (drought resistance as a proportional change)
checks.note: More diverse communities 'more resistant to' the drought; resistance was measured as the proportional (log ratio) change in biomass.

checks.claim: Key: each species lost hurt more than the one before it
checks.note: Abstract: 'The curvilinear relationship we observe suggests that each additional species lost from our grasslands had a progressively greater impact on drought resistance.'

checks.claim: Wrong choices: each lost hurt less than the one before / about as much as any other / the first few did no harm at all
checks.note: All contradict the 'progressively greater impact' finding. 'No harm at all' is the redundancy idea the paper rejected; the saturating curve gives the first losses a small, not zero, cost in the authors' reading.

checks.claim: Context: support for the diversity-stability idea, against most species being functionally redundant
checks.note: Abstract: results 'support the diversity-stability hypothesis, but not the alternative hypothesis that most species are functionally redundant'.

checks.claim: Context: critics noted nitrogen fertilizer added to many plots had cut their species and changed their growth
checks.note: Huston 1997, 'Hidden treatments in ecological experiments' (search snippet): the Cedar Creek study is not a direct test because richness 'was not manipulated directly but was a product of changes in nitrogen addition'. N addition lowers richness and raises biomass (Cedar Creek e001).

checks.claim: Context: the two found the pattern held when they allowed for nitrogen
checks.note: Tilman, Isbell and Cowles 2014 (Annu. Rev. Ecol. Evol. Syst.), per search snippet: the diversity effect 'remained highly significant even after the paper's authors statistically controlled for many potentially confounding variables, including rates of nitrogen addition and species composition'. (The page itself returned 403; the passage was read in the search index.)

checks.claim: Context: a 2017 reanalysis disputes this
checks.note: ESA 2017 meeting abstract (page unreachable from here; its text was read in the search index): 'Accounting for differences among communities due to nitrogen treatment, the authors find no effect of richness on drought resistance. Instead, nitrogen treatment was the primary driver, as Huston suggested.' A meeting abstract, not a peer-reviewed paper, so 'disputes' is the right weight. The context is fair to both sides: it gives the finding, the critics' point, the authors' control, and the dissent, with no verdict.

checks.claim: David Tilman, 207 grassland plots at Cedar Creek, followed year after year
checks.note: Tilman 1996, 'Biodiversity: population versus ecosystem stability', Ecology 77:350-363: 207 grassland plots over 11 years.

checks.claim: Stem: in species-rich plots each species rose and fell more from year to year
checks.note: Lecture summary of Tilman 1996: 'Year to year variability in species abundance higher in species rich plots'. The abstract itself says species abundances were not stabilized by richness and that compensatory increases 'cause species abundances to be more variable'. Fair at grade level.

checks.claim: Stem: total plant mass of rich plots held steadier
checks.note: Year-to-year variability in total aboveground biomass 'significantly lower in plots with greater plant species richness'.

checks.claim: Key: when some species did badly, others grew to fill in
checks.note: Abstract: when climatic variations harm some species, unharmed competitors increase; 'Such compensatory increases stabilize total community biomass'; the difference likely results from interspecific competition.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: all their species rose and fell together
checks.note: Wrong: stability comes from asynchrony ('This asynchrony stabilizes aggregate ecosystem productivity even when individual species vary widely'); synchrony would make the total swing more.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: their species stopped competing for water and light
checks.note: Wrong: Tilman attributes the pattern to interspecific competition, not its absence.

checks.claim: Wrong choice: the weather over them swung less from year to year
checks.note: Wrong: the plots share one site and one climate.

checks.claim: Context: the insurance effect (more species, likelier some thrive in any year's weather)
checks.note: Insurance hypothesis (Yachi and Loreau 1999): 'biodiversity buffers ecosystem functioning against environmental fluctuations' through redundancy and asynchrony.

checks.claim: Zhu Youyong's team, Yunnan, whole townships, 1998 and 1999
checks.note: Zhu et al., 'Genetic diversity and disease control in rice', Nature 406:718-722 (2000): diversified rice 'planted in all the rice fields in five townships in 1998 and ten townships in 1999'.

checks.claim: Single rows of sticky (glutinous) rice between four or six rows of a hybrid rice that blast seldom harms
checks.note: Zhu et al. 2001: 'a repeating pattern of one row of glutinous rice interplanted with four or six rows of indica rice'; glutinous Huangkenuo and Zinuo 'highly susceptible', indica hybrids Xianyou 63 or 22 'generally resistant'.

checks.claim: Blast on the sticky rice fell by 94 percent; blast is caused by a fungus
checks.note: Susceptible varieties in mixtures: 89% greater yield, blast 94% less severe than in monoculture. Rice blast is the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae.

checks.claim: Key: most spores now met plants the fungus could not infect (dilution)
checks.note: Dilution of inoculum between compatible hosts 'has been considered the most important mechanism in variety mixtures' (Raboin et al. 2012, citing Wolfe 1985 and Mundt 2002). Best of the four offered.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: more fungicide / resistance caught from the hybrid / hybrid took the water the fungus needed
checks.note: All wrong as worded: spraying stopped; resistance genes do not pass between plants; the drier leaves of the sticky rice (below) come from its standing 35-40 cm above the hybrid canopy, not from the hybrid taking water. 'Took the water' sits near a real mechanism, but its wording is clearly wrong.

checks.claim: Context: dilution given as the whole explanation
checks.note: Zhu et al. 2005 (Phytopathology 95:433-438) on these same mixtures: the glutinous rice was '35 to 40 cm taller'; days at 100% humidity at its panicles fell from 20.0 to 2.2, dew cover from 84% to 36%; 'Although other mechanisms also were operative, reduced leaf wetness was likely a substantial contributor'. The context is not false but tells only half the story. Fix: after the dilution sentence add 'The taller sticky rice, standing above the hybrid, also dried faster after the morning dew, and the fungus needs wet leaves.'

checks.claim: Context: 'Resistance is inherited in a plant's genes and is never caught from a neighbour'
checks.note: Induced resistance is one of the three textbook mechanisms of variety mixtures: 'triggered by the presence of avirulent spores in the crop that induce the expression of the plant defence mechanisms' (spores often from the neighbouring variety). So 'never caught' is too absolute for a plant pathologist. Fix: 'A plant's resistance genes come from its parents; they never pass to a plant growing beside it.'

checks.claim: Context: by the end of the two years farmers no longer needed fungicide
checks.note: Abstract: fungicide sprays no longer needed by the end of the two-year programme.

checks.claim: Phytophthora infestans is a water mould (oomycete), not a true fungus
checks.note: 'Distinct from true fungi, P. infestans belongs to the stramenopile kingdom'; cellulose cell walls.

checks.claim: It reached Ireland in 1845 and rotted fields across the island
checks.note: First observations in Ireland late August / early September 1845; about one-third of the 1845 crop destroyed by harvest time, nearly all of 1846's.

checks.claim: Much of the crop was one variety, the Lumper, grown from tubers, genetically uniform, with no resistance
checks.note: The 'high-yielding but genetically uniform Irish Lumper'; 'its genetic uniformity heightened vulnerability to disease'; varieties 'lacking genetic resistance'. Tuber-grown plants are clones (Grokipedia, Potato).

checks.claim: Key: breeders found resistance genes in wild potato species of Mexico
checks.note: R1-R11 came from Solanum demissum (Grokipedia, P. infestans), native to 'Mexico and Guatemala' and 'extensively used as a source of alleles for resistance to Phytophthora infestans'. Most Rpi genes come from tuber-bearing wild species, nine of them from Mexico (PMC9110483).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: old Irish varieties / seedlings from Lumper seed / potatoes sprayed for years
checks.note: Irish varieties of the time lacked resistance; the Lumper had none to pass on; spraying does not change inherited genes.

checks.claim: Context: eleven genes R1 to R11 from S. demissum; the mould has since overcome every one; breeders now stack several, many from other wild species
checks.note: 'Rpi genes introduced from S. demissum were quickly overcome'; isolate 2013-18-306 overcomes R1, R2, R3a, R3b, R4-R11; pyramiding several Rpi genes is the current approach (S. bulbocastanum, S. venturii, S. stoloniferum).

checks.claim: Ricketts' team, a large Costa Rican coffee farm, sites beside forest and up to 1.6 km away
checks.note: Ricketts, Daily, Ehrlich and Michener, PNAS 101:12579-12582 (2004): Finca Santa Fe, 1,065 ha, Valle General; near sites within 100 m, far sites 1,400-1,600 m.

checks.claim: Some branches hand-pollinated, others left alone; near the forest both set about the same crop; far away hand-dusted set about a fifth more
checks.note: Branches on the same plants split between treatments. Near and intermediate: 'neither seed mass nor fruit set increased with hand-pollination'. Far: seed mass +8.3%, fruit set +11.5%, together +20.8%.

checks.claim: Key: 'Bees from the forest reached only the nearer bushes'
checks.note: Overstated. Bees did reach the far sites ('bees must fly farther from forest patches to reach far sites'); bee richness and visit rate fell with distance, and 'stigmas received hundreds of pollen grains even in distant sites'. Fix: 'Bees from the forest seldom reached the far bushes' (the three wrong choices can keep their 'reached only the nearer bushes' form).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: water / shade / pests from the forest
checks.note: Wrong: both treatments were on the same plants at each site, so water, shade or pests touched both alike; only pollination differed.

checks.claim: Context: 'Far away the flowers got too little pollen, so extra pollen helped'
checks.note: The authors reject this: far stigmas still got hundreds of grains, and 'Simple relief from pollen limitation is thus unlikely to account for the effects we found.' They suggest pollen QUALITY (fewer, later visits bring less pollen from other bushes; native bees cross-pollinate better) and timing. Fix: 'Far away fewer bees came, and later, so fewer flowers got the pollen from other bushes that sets the best beans; the hand-dusting supplied it.'

checks.claim: Context: coffee can self-pollinate but bee visits raise its crop; feral honeybees and ten native stingless bees
checks.note: C. arabica 'is able to self-pollinate', bee visits raise yields 15-50%; dominant visitors feral Africanized honey bees and 10 native stingless bee species. 'Lived in the forest' matches the paper's 'forest-based pollinators' (the farm's shade trees lacked nesting cavities).

checks.claim: Context: about 20% yield within a kilometre, 27% fewer misshapen beans, about $60,000 a year
checks.note: Abstract: yields +20% within about 1 km; peaberries cut by 27%; about $60,000 a year (Results: $62,000 from patches A and B).

checks.claim: Lucas Garibaldi and dozens of colleagues, 41 crop systems worldwide
checks.note: Garibaldi et al., Science 339:1608-1611 (2013), about 50 authors; 600 fields on every continent but Antarctica, 41 crop systems.

checks.claim: Visits by wild insects and by honeybees from managed hives, and fruit set, counted in each field
checks.note: The abstract speaks of 'managed honey bees'; honey bees were counted apart from wild insects. (Some honey bees in some regions were feral, but the paper frames them as managed.)

checks.claim: Key: wild insect visits raised fruit set about twice as much
checks.note: 'an increase in wild insect visitation enhanced fruit set by twice as much as an equivalent increase in honey bee visitation'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: honeybees twice as much / both equal / wild insects mattered only where honeybees were few
checks.note: All contradict the abstract; the title says wild pollinators enhance fruit set 'regardless of honey bee abundance'.

checks.claim: Context: positive in all 41 systems; honeybees clearly helped in only 14%; hives supplement rather than replace wild pollinators
checks.note: 'universally positive associations ... in 41 crop systems'; significant for honey bees 'in only 14% of the systems surveyed'; managed honey bees 'supplemented, rather than substituted for, pollination by wild insects'.

checks.claim: Stem: in 1970 each hybrid was grown from seed of a cross between two inbred parent lines
checks.note: Not true of every 1970 hybrid. 'Double-cross hybrids were primarily grown across the United States from the 1930s through the 1960s', and the shift to single crosses (two inbreds) was finished only by the early 1970s. Many 1970 hybrids were double or three-way crosses of four or three inbreds (Michigan State's 1970 trial bulletin lists most entries as double crosses: https://archive.lib.msu.edu/DMC/extension_publications/e431/e431-1970.pdf). Fix: 'each grown from seed of a cross between inbred parent lines' (drop 'two').

checks.claim: Race T, a new race of a fungus, spread through the Corn Belt and cut the harvest by about 15 percent
checks.note: Bipolaris maydis (Cochliobolus heterostrophus) race T; about 15% (710 million bushels, about $1 billion); Wikipedia: 'about 15% of the corn belt's crop'. (Some sources say 16%; 'about 15' holds.)

checks.claim: Key: most carried the same inherited trait that race T attacked (Texas male-sterile cytoplasm)
checks.note: About 85% (Grokipedia; Bruns 2017: '>85% of the hybrids') to 90% (Wikipedia) of US hybrids carried T-cms; race T's T-toxin targets the T-urf13 protein in T-cms mitochondria. The cytoplasm is inherited through the mother.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: copies of one plant / race T attacked every corn equally / race T built up for decades
checks.note: Hybrids come from crosses, not clones; race T's toxin is specific to T-cms corn; race T was new (first in the Philippines 1961, in the US 1968-69).

checks.claim: Context: T-cms bred in to make hybrid seed without hand detasseling; 85 to 90 percent; corn without it held up; danger passed by 1972 with the return to normal cytoplasm
checks.note: Adopted 'to eliminate the previous need for hand detasseling'; by 1971 about half of seed was normal cytoplasm, resolved by 1972 (Grokipedia); Bruns 2017: 'The cms-T was discontinued in 1971'.

checks.claim: Context: race T had first appeared only in 1969
checks.note: Sources differ: Bruns 2017 ('first appeared in the Corn Belt in 1969') and Grokipedia (Florida, 1969) say 1969; Wikipedia says the disease 'first appeared in the U.S. in 1968'. Safer: 'race T had appeared only a year or two before'.

checks.claim: Short experiments, most about two years long, had found more than six or eight species gave no further benefit
checks.note: 'Prior shorter-term studies, most about two years long' had found 'having more than six or eight species in a plot gave no additional benefit'.

checks.claim: Peter Reich's team, Cedar Creek plots sown with 1 to 16 prairie species, followed more than a decade
checks.note: Reich et al., Science 336:589-592 (2012), lead author Peter Reich; two Cedar Creek experiments with plots of 'one, four, nine or 16' species; 13-14 years.

checks.claim: Key: each added species raised soil fertility and plant growth
checks.note: 'every additional species in a plot contributed to a gradual increase in both soil fertility and biomass production'. Abstract: diversity effects 'increased and became less saturating over time'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: beyond eight added nothing / richest plots grew less / helped only in drought years
checks.note: All contradict the finding that diversity effects grew over time and that high-diversity mixes, redundant in early years, became functionally unique later.

checks.claim: Context: species gather water, nutrients and carbon in different ways; spare-seeming species prove their worth over a decade
checks.note: 'different species have different ways to acquire water, nutrients and carbon and maintain them in the ecosystem'; species 'appeared functionally redundant during early years' (abstract).

unit_notes: Two errors and one uncertain. 4f4644d10a (Ricketts coffee): the key overstates ('reached only') and the context's 'too little pollen' is the explanation the paper itself rejects (far stigmas got hundreds of grains; the authors point to pollen quality and timing). 7139561bbd (1970 corn blight): 'each ... a cross between two inbred parent lines' is false for 1970, when double-cross hybrids were still widely grown; drop 'two'. Its date for race T (1969) is split 1968/1969 across sources. b1c6da2fa3 (Yunnan rice): key and choices are fine, but the context gives dilution as the whole story when Zhu et al. 2005 found the taller sticky rice's drier leaves a substantial contributor, and 'never caught from a neighbour' is too absolute given induced resistance; fixes in the checks. The 2017 ESA reanalysis (eco.confex.com) could not be opened directly; its text was read in the search index and matches the context. The Tilman and Downing context is fair to both sides.
